title: Vitamin B12 and folate deficiency (adult)
subject: haematology-oncology
summary: Test when a symptom and a risk factor coexist. Treat B12 deficiency with IM hydroxocobalamin 1 mg (three times weekly for 2 weeks, or alternate days if neurological, then every 2 to 3 months) or oral B12 at least 1 mg daily where suitable; never give folic acid alone until B12 deficiency is excluded or treated.

sections.title: Recognise
items: Features: anaemia or macrocytosis (deficiency can occur without either), fatigue, glossitis, poor concentration or memory, depression, anxiety or psychosis, paraesthesia and peripheral neuropathy, ataxia and falls from impaired proprioception (subacute combined degeneration), visual loss from optic neuropathy.

B12 risk factors: diet low in animal foods without fortified foods or supplements (vegan or vegetarian, including for religious reasons), autoimmune gastritis or other autoimmune disease, gastrectomy, bariatric surgery, ileal resection, coeliac disease.

Drug and other B12 risk factors: metformin, PPIs, H2 blockers, colchicine, some antiepileptics (phenobarbital, primidone, topiramate), pregabalin, recreational nitrous oxide, previous abdominal or pelvic radiotherapy.
Offer testing when at least 1 symptom or sign and at least 1 risk factor are present; use judgement if there is a symptom but no risk factor (NICE NG239).

Folate deficiency: poor diet, alcohol excess, malabsorption (coeliac disease), increased demand (pregnancy, haemolysis, exfoliative skin disease, dialysis), and drugs (methotrexate, trimethoprim, phenytoin and other antiepileptics).

sections.title: Investigations
items: CBC and blood film (macrocytosis, hypersegmented neutrophils), reticulocytes, ferritin; severe megaloblastic anaemia can cause pancytopenia and raised LDH and bilirubin. Take samples before any replacement.

Total B12 below 180 ng/L (133 pmol/L) or active B12 (holotranscobalamin) below 25 pmol/L confirms deficiency; 180 to 350 ng/L (133 to 258 pmol/L) or 25 to 70 pmol/L is indeterminate (NICE). Use local laboratory cut-offs where they differ.
Indeterminate result with symptoms: measure serum methylmalonic acid (or homocysteine). Use active B12 in pregnancy, and MMA or homocysteine first when nitrous oxide use is suspected.

Find the cause: anti-intrinsic factor antibodies (a negative result does not exclude autoimmune gastritis; consider parietal cell antibodies, gastrin or gastroscopy), coeliac serology if still unexplained, medication and diet review.
Folate: serum folate is the first-line test; below 7 nmol/L (3 micrograms/L) indicates deficiency (BSH). Always check B12 at the same time.

sections.title: Vitamin B12 replacement
items: Megaloblastic anaemia with neurological symptoms: do not wait for results; start IM hydroxocobalamin straight after taking blood.

No neurological involvement: hydroxocobalamin 1 mg IM three times a week for 2 weeks, then 1 mg every 3 months. Neurological involvement: 1 mg IM on alternate days until no further improvement, then 1 mg every 2 months, with urgent haematology or neurology advice.

Lifelong IM replacement for autoimmune gastritis, total gastrectomy or complete terminal ileal resection. Other malabsorption (coeliac disease, partial gastrectomy, bariatric surgery): consider IM, or oral at least 1 mg daily.

Dietary deficiency: dietary advice and oral cyanocobalamin (at least 1 mg daily in pregnancy or breastfeeding); IM if neurological or haematological disease could deteriorate quickly, or adherence is a concern.
Medicine-induced (metformin, PPI) or nitrous oxide-related deficiency: oral or IM replacement, review the medicine, and advise stopping nitrous oxide.
If only cyanocobalamin injection is available, it is retained less well and given more often (for example 1 mg IM daily or on alternate days for 1 to 2 weeks, then weekly, then monthly).

sections.title: Folate replacement and prevention
items: Folic acid 5 mg orally daily for 4 months (longer if the cause persists), only once B12 deficiency is excluded or B12 treatment has started: folic acid alone can precipitate or worsen subacute combined degeneration.
If both are low, or results are pending in megaloblastic anaemia, give hydroxocobalamin first or together with folic acid.

Neural tube defect prevention: folic acid 400 micrograms daily from before conception to 12 weeks; 5 mg daily if high risk (previous NTD, diabetes, antiepileptic drugs, BMI 30 or more, sickle cell disease, malabsorption).

sections.title: Response and follow-up
items: Reticulocytosis peaks at about day 7 and haemoglobin rises within 1 to 2 weeks, normalising over about 8 weeks; neurological recovery is slower and may be incomplete.
Severe anaemia: check potassium in the first days of treatment (hypokalaemia can occur); avoid transfusion unless there is cardiovascular compromise, and then transfuse slowly with diuretic cover.

First follow-up at 3 months (1 month in pregnancy or breastfeeding) to review symptoms. Poor response on oral B12: increase to the maximum licensed dose or switch to IM. Do not repeat B12 levels on IM treatment.
Haemoglobin stalls if iron deficiency coexists: check ferritin.
Autoimmune gastritis carries a higher risk of gastric neuroendocrine tumours and possibly adenocarcinoma: refer for endoscopy if new or worsening upper GI symptoms.

sections.title: Pregnancy and older adults
items: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: test with active B12; if autoimmune gastritis is suspected start IM replacement without waiting for antibody results; continue replacement started before pregnancy.
Older adults: cognitive decline, falls or neuropathy may be the only features; treat and review rather than attributing them to age.
Metformin users: check B12 if neuropathy develops before attributing it to diabetes.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Giving folic acid alone to a patient with unrecognised B12 deficiency.
Excluding deficiency because there is no anaemia or macrocytosis; neurological damage can occur without them.
Stopping IM injections in autoimmune gastritis once symptoms improve: replacement is lifelong.
Misreading B12 levels in people taking over-the-counter B12 (falsely reassuring) or the combined pill (falsely low).
Missing recreational nitrous oxide use in a young person with myelopathy or neuropathy; serum B12 may be normal, so check MMA or homocysteine.

drugs.name: Hydroxocobalamin
drugs.dose: 1 mg IM three times weekly for 2 weeks, then 1 mg every 3 months; with neurological involvement 1 mg IM on alternate days until no further improvement, then 1 mg every 2 months
drugs.notes: Lifelong in autoimmune gastritis, total gastrectomy or terminal ileal resection.

drugs.name: Cyanocobalamin (oral)
drugs.dose: 1 mg orally daily for malabsorption or in pregnancy and breastfeeding; 50 to 150 micrograms daily can suffice for purely dietary deficiency
drugs.notes: Increase to the maximum licensed dose or switch to IM if response is poor.

drugs.name: Folic acid (treatment)
drugs.dose: 5 mg orally daily for 4 months; if the cause persists, 5 mg every 1 to 7 days
drugs.notes: Only when B12 is replete or being replaced.

drugs.name: Folic acid (neural tube defect prevention)
drugs.dose: 400 micrograms orally daily from before conception to 12 weeks; 5 mg daily if high risk
drugs.notes: High risk: previous NTD, diabetes, antiepileptic drugs, BMI 30 or more, sickle cell disease, malabsorption.
